blocks.content: Copy-on-write is the mechanism that lets many containers share the exact same read-only image layers safely, a file is only ever actually duplicated the moment a container tries to modify it, never before.
1. Unmodified Files Are Read Directly, Shared
blocks.text: 1. Unmodified Files Are Read Directly, Shared

blocks.content: As long as a container never touches a particular file, it reads that file directly from the shared, read-only lowerdir layer, exactly as covered in the OverlayFS topic, no copying happens at all, and every other container using that same image layer reads the identical, shared data.

blocks.alt: No copying at all, for anything the container never touches

blocks.content: The moment a container attempts to modify a file that currently only exists in a lower, read-only layer, OverlayFS performs a copy-up: it copies that file into the container's own upperdir first, and only then applies the write, to that new copy, the original in the lower layer is never touched.

blocks.alt: The file is copied up before the write is ever applied

blocks.content: 3. The Whole File, Not Just a Diff
blocks.text: 3. The Whole File, Not Just a Diff

blocks.content: It is worth knowing precisely what gets copied, a copy-up duplicates the entire file into upperdir, not just the specific bytes being changed, a one-byte edit to a large file still means the whole file gets copied up first.

blocks.alt: An entire file copied, regardless of how small the actual edit is

blocks.content: This is exactly the mechanism behind two properties covered earlier in this course: containers start instantly because nothing needs to be copied upfront, and many containers running the same image share disk space efficiently, since unmodified data is never duplicated, only ever what each container actually changes.

blocks.alt: Instant starts and shared disk space, both from the same mechanism

blocks.content: This has a genuine practical cost: a workload that frequently modifies a large file originally sitting in a lower layer pays a real, repeated copy-up cost. Applications with this pattern (databases writing directly into a path that started in the image, for instance) are a strong argument for using an explicit volume, covered in the Docker Volumes module, instead of writing into the ordinary layered filesystem.

blocks.alt: Frequent modification of a large lower-layer file has a real, repeated cost

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Copy-on-write means a file is only ever duplicated the instant a container modifies it, unmodified files are read directly from the shared lower layer.
A copy-up duplicates the entire file, not a diff, which is exactly why frequently-modified large files are a strong signal to use a volume instead.
